title: Data Desk
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the data chapter. An adult sees a table being filled in. What is actually being settled is that data is facts collected to give information, and that a table puts each number under its own name, so it can be found, compared and added. The recap on the opening pages reads a pictograph of sixes with a key of three, and a child who skips the key writes the number of pictures as the number of sixes. The section headed Data Collection only sets out data that was already collected; this tool starts by collecting it.

writeup.why: Collect facts that give information, set them out in a table under their names, read a pictograph row with its key, and find the most, the least, the same and the total.
writeup.look: A desk with a drawn class along its top edge, a heap of answer slips, a ruled table in the middle, and a pictograph board that slides over it with a compare rail beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Data Desk' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the answers collected, the slips placed, the symbols counted in the row being read, or the rows placed on the rail, against what this phase holds, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each child answers, each slip lands, each symbol is counted or each row takes its place, and the second is fixed at what this phase holds. The symbols of a row are counted here and nowhere else. The row's number is written at the end of its row, so a count of pictures and the number it stands for never share a place. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The class row runs along the top of the working area: up to thirty drawn children, each 32 by 88 with 3 between, at 64,210, reaching 1111. The class is line drawing in near-black ink on the panel colour, so no child is mistaken for a symbol. A child who has answered carries a small tick at their feet and cannot be asked twice. Tapping a child drops their answer onto the desk as a slip, a card 96 by 36 with the answer's name on it. It lands in the slip heap, a tray 220 by 330 at 64,322. The table stands to the right of the heap: up to six heading cells, each 110 by 64, in a row at 300,330, and a number cell 110 by 72 under each at 300,394. The total cell, 130 by 136, stands at the table's end at 960,330. A slip dragged to a column slides under its heading, and the number in that column climbs by one in amber. The total cell adds the numbers under the headings and writes the sum in reddish purple. The check strip under the table, 790 by 56 at 300,482, stands the count of slips in the heap beside it. The total cell's label says answers, and it says children only when each child gave one answer. The pictograph board, 820 by 340 at 300,322, slides in over the table from the right. A title strip 620 by 44 runs along its top, and the key card stands at 930,322, 190 by 80, showing one symbol and what it stands for. Up to six rows stand below from 412, each 36 tall with 6 between. Each row has its name in a cell 130 wide at the left, then its symbols from 440, each 36 wide with 8 between, up to ten. Its number, with its unit, sits in a tag 90 wide just beyond its last symbol. Tapping a row lays the pale sky blue band behind it. The row reader then counts its symbols into the running count one at a time. It takes the key's value once under each symbol in amber, and the row's number lands in its tag. The compare rail runs under the board, 820 by 56 at 300,670, with up to six places for the rows' numbers, the largest at the left and the smallest at the right. Two equal numbers share one place, side by side under one near-black bracket. Tapping two numbers on the rail lights both rows on the board and lays the sky blue band behind the symbols by which the longer row passes the shorter. That stretch is counted and read with the key, and its size is written on the band. The total bar sits at the lower left, 220 by 56 at 64,670, and adds every row once when the question asks for all of them. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a count or a number is asked for. A word pad carries this desk's own words: the row names of the board or the table, and most, least, same, more and in all. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and every fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in the rows, is green, except where the rows are named by colour. There each row's symbols wear that row's own colour: red, green, blue, yellow or purple. The key's symbol there is plain grey, which stands for one symbol of any colour and is used for nothing else. Amber is what a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, and so are the numbers in a table and the numbers a side ruler writes. Amber too is what half a symbol stands for, what a key leaves over, and a small round counter for one thing counted. A total of every row is reddish purple, and so is a thing a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share. The row a question asks about is marked by a pale sky blue band laid behind its symbols, never over them. So is the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another. Chrome never borrows one of those, and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every table rule, row line, belt, route line, bracket, outlined blank and card edge is near-black, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. Every reading survives with the colour taken away. A fifth mark lies across and not upright, and a half symbol is the left half of the whole. A row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it. No amount is ever drawn as a length of colour: an amount on this stage is symbols, marks, counters or a written number. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. A count of symbols sits in the running count, and a row's number sits at its row's end. A sum of rows sits in the total cell or the total bar and nowhere else. The number a row stands for is never written in the corner, and a sum of rows is never written beside a single row.
writeup.finish: The card shows the table the child made from the answers they collected, with its total, and the pictograph rows standing on the compare rail in order.

phases.win: the last slip lands and the question card turns to show what the heap tells
phases.does: taps each child, watches the answer drop as a slip, then says what the heap of slips can tell the school
phases.goal: facts collected to give useful information are data, and each fact has a name that says what was counted
phases.says: Ask each child. What can all these answers tell the school?
phases.check: Away from the screen: ask five friends their favourite fruit. Write each answer down with its name.
phases.feels: each answer arrives with its name on it, one child at a time, and the heap grows by one
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, ask the class how they came to school, and mark each answer on the board as it comes. Then write four numbers on the board with no names beside them, and ask what they tell anyone. Write the names back and ask again. The section headed Data Collection defines data and then only sets out data already collected, so let the class collect some first. Four numbers with no names tell nobody what was counted.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does each number count? Second rung, the phase's: what could the school learn from these answers? Third rung: the class is cut to three children, and the child collects their three slips and says what they tell. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the numbers look just like the counts collected a minute ago, and a number seems to be the fact all by itself.
wrong.move: calls four numbers written with no names data about the class, and says what each one means.
wrong.screen: the four numbers stay on the desk as the child left them. The question card asks which of them is the bus. One at a time, each slip's name is drawn back beside its number, and the card is answered only once the names are back. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: weather reports are given as examples of data, and a picture of rain looks like part of one.
wrong.move: calls a drawing of a rain cloud data, because rain is in the weather reports the section names.
wrong.screen: the drawing is set beside the slip heap, and the question card asks how many. The heap answers with a count for each name. The drawing gives no count and no name, so nothing from it lands in the table, and it stays where the child put it.

wrong.why: a heap that grows looks like more data, and the child's answer is still a true answer.
wrong.move: taps a child who has already answered, to add their answer a second time.
wrong.screen: the child is drawn with the small tick at their feet and gives no second slip. The running count stays level with the children asked, and the heap stays as it was.

phases.screen: a drawn class along the top of the desk, an empty heap and a question card asking how each child came to school
phases.soWhat: Facts collected to give useful information are data, and each carries a name that says what was counted.

phases.win: the heap empties into the columns and the total cell matches the number of slips collected
phases.does: drags each slip into the column for its name, then fills the total cell
phases.goal: a table puts each number under its own name, and the numbers add up to the whole group
phases.says: Where does this answer belong? Now add the columns. Does the total match the heap?
phases.check: Four friends each pick one colour. Make a table. Does its total match the friends?
phases.feels: every slip slides under its own heading, and the columns add up to the heap they came from
phases.hands: Set the class's answers out on the board as a table, a heading for each way of coming to school and the number of children under it. Add the numbers, then count the children who were asked, and let the class see that the two match. Say why: each child gave one answer. Then ask each child for exactly two favourite games and add that table; its sum is twice the children. The chapter's own table heads its row team where the text says house, and lists the houses in another order. Every value agrees, so read it by the names.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what name is on this slip? Second rung, the phase's: do the columns add up to the heap? Third rung: the heap is cut to five slips under two headings, and the child places each one and adds the two numbers. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: the headings are the first thing in the table to count, and the numbers under them look like labels.
wrong.move: counts the headings instead of adding the numbers, and says there are four children because there are four seasons.
wrong.screen: the four heading cells are counted into the running count, and the child's four stays in the slot. The total cell then adds the numbers under them, six, nine, eight and five, one at a time, and twenty-eight lands. Each child chose one season, so the cell is labelled children, and the check strip stands the heap's twenty-eight slips beside it.

wrong.why: the columns stand close together, and the hand goes back to the column the last slip went into.
wrong.move: drops a slip into the column beside its name, so one column is one too many and its neighbour one too few.
wrong.screen: the column's slips fan out under their heading, each showing its name. The one whose name is not the heading's is lifted clear and turned so its name faces both headings. It stays where the child put it until the child moves it.

wrong.why: every total met so far has been the number of children, because every child so far gave one answer.
wrong.move: adds a table in which each child named two games, and calls the sum the number of children.
wrong.screen: the total cell matches the heap, twenty-four slips. The class row then shows its twelve children, each with two slips drawn from them, and the total cell's label reads answers, not children.

phases.screen: the heap of slips beside a ruled table with a heading for each answer and every number cell empty
phases.soWhat: A table puts each number under its own name, and its numbers add up to the children when each child gave one answer.
phases.concept: Setting data out in a table

phases.win: the key's value is taken once for each symbol and the row's number lands at the end of the row
phases.does: counts the symbols in the lit row, reads the key, and writes the row's number with its unit
phases.goal: a pictograph row is read by counting its symbols and taking the key that many times
phases.says: Count the pictures in this row. What does one picture stand for?
phases.check: One picture stands for four books. How many books do six pictures show?
phases.feels: each picture holds the same amount, and the row is that amount taken once for every picture
phases.hands: Draw one row of a pictograph on the board, five mango pictures, with a key of one picture for six mangoes. Ask how many mangoes, and wait for someone to say five. Then take the key once for each picture aloud: six, twelve, eighteen, twenty-four, thirty. The recap's pictograph of sixes has a key of one bat for three sixes, and its questions ask for sixes, not bats. So every row there is turned into sixes with the key before an answer is given.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pictures are in the row? Second rung, the phase's: what does one picture stand for? Third rung: the row is cut to two symbols, and the child takes the key twice. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: counting the pictures is the first thing done to a row, and the count looks like the answer.
wrong.move: writes the number of pictures as the answer, five mangoes, without using the key.
wrong.screen: the running count holds the five symbols. The row reader then takes the key's six once under each symbol in amber, climbing to thirty, which lands in the row's tag. The child's five stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the rows are close together, and a finger sliding along a row can drift onto its neighbour.
wrong.move: reads the row above or below the one the question names.
wrong.screen: the lit row keeps its sky blue band. The row the child read is outlined, and its name is set beside the name the question gives. The row reader then counts the lit row's symbols one at a time.

wrong.why: the key card shows a number, and it is the only number printed anywhere near the row.
wrong.move: writes the key's own number, six, as the row's number.
wrong.screen: the row reader takes the six under the first symbol only and stops, with the tag reading six. It then carries on under each symbol in turn, and the tag climbs to thirty.

phases.screen: the pictograph board over the table, with its title strip and key card, and one row lit
phases.soWhat: A pictograph row is read by counting its symbols and taking the key that many times.
phases.concept: Reading a pictograph with its key

phases.win: the rows stand in order on the rail, two equal numbers level with each other, and the total fills the bar
phases.does: stands the rows on the compare rail, names the most, the least and the two that are equal, then taps the total bar
phases.goal: the most and the least come from comparing the numbers, and the total from adding every row once
phases.says: Which is the most? Which is the least? Which two are the same? Now add them all.
phases.check: Rows stand for eighteen, twelve and nine. Which is the least, and how many more is eighteen than nine?
phases.feels: the rows stand in order on the rail, and a difference is the stretch by which one row passes another
phases.hands: Read a pictograph with the class: which row is the most, which the least, and which two are the same. Then ask how many more one row has than another, and take the smaller from the larger. A question worded as how many children like one thing more than another means how many more chose it, so ask it that way. The recap asks how many sixes all five players hit together. There adding every row is what the question asks, and each six was hit by one player only.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is the largest? Second rung, the phase's: are two of the numbers the same? Third rung: the board is cut to two rows, and the child lines them up and counts the stars the longer row has left. The number keys and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: adding every row is right for in all, and the stars are what the eye has been counting.
wrong.move: adds the stars, twenty-one, and gives that as the number of stickers in all.
wrong.screen: the running count holds the twenty-one stars. The total bar then adds the rows' numbers, twenty, thirty-two, twelve and twenty, and eighty-four lands in the bar. Each sticker was collected by one class, so the bar is labelled stickers in all. The child's twenty-one stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the question names two rows, and joining two numbers has always meant adding them.
wrong.move: adds the two numbers when the question asks how many more, giving forty-four for thirty-two and twelve.
wrong.screen: the two numbers are tapped on the rail and both rows light on the board. The sky blue band lies behind the five stars by which the longer row passes the shorter, and they are read with the key, twenty. The child's forty-four stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the question names the first thing first, and its number is the one the eye finds.
wrong.move: answers a question worded as how many children like one thing more than another with the first thing's whole count.
wrong.screen: the question card turns to its other face, which asks how many more chose the first thing than the second. The two rows are lined up on the board, and the stretch by which the first passes the second is banded and counted.

phases.screen: the pictograph board with every row's number written, the compare rail empty and the total bar waiting
phases.soWhat: Read the most, the least and the same from the numbers. How many more is the smaller taken from the larger.
phases.concept: Most, least, equal and in all

writeup.delight: The second phase, once the total cell matches the heap. The children in the class row give a small wave one at a time from the left. Each waves as their own slip is found in its column and lights there for a moment. A child who gave two answers waves twice, once for each slip. It runs as often as a finger likes on the total cell, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the drawn class stands along the top of the desk and the slip heap is empty. The question card asking how each child came to school sits in the slot. On the second the heap is full, and the table stands beside it with a heading cell for each answer, every number cell empty and the total cell empty. On the third the pictograph board has slid over the table, its title strip and key card showing and one row lit. On the fourth the same board stands with every row's number written, the compare rail empty under it and the total bar waiting at the left. The running count at the top left holds what this phase has done so far against what it holds, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once, while the voice asks its question: the first child in the class row, or the top slip of the heap, or the lit row, or the largest row's number, gives one slow pulse. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any class of up to thirty children and any question put to them, with the table, the pictograph board, the compare rail and the total bar all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on what data is, setting data out in a table and finding its total, reading a pictograph row with its key, and finding the most, the least, the same and the total.
voiceLines: A class along the top, and an empty table on the desk. Ask each child.

Where does this answer belong? Now add the columns. Does the total match the heap?
Count the pictures in this row. What does one picture stand for?
Which is the most? Which is the least? Which two are the same? Now add them all.
Another question. Read the names before you read the numbers.
Free play. Any class and any question, with the table and the board open.
Read the name at the top of the column, and count that row again.
Answers collected, set out under their names, read with the key, and compared.

observations.why: A child who has answered cannot be asked again, and nobody was skipped.
observations.soWhat: Data is collected one fact at a time, and each fact carries the name of what it is.
observations.observe: Every child in the class row gave one slip, and the heap's count matched the children asked.

observations.why: Adding the columns counts every slip once, and a child who gave two answers put two slips in the heap.
observations.soWhat: A table's numbers add up to the children when each child gave one answer, and to the answers otherwise.
observations.observe: The total cell matched the heap of slips every time, and the heap matched the class when each child gave one answer.

observations.why: Each symbol stood for six mangoes, so six was taken once under each symbol.
observations.soWhat: A pictograph row is its symbols counted and the key taken that many times.
observations.observe: The row reader counted five symbols into the corner, and thirty landed at the row's end.

observations.why: The rail puts the rows in order by their numbers, so equal numbers take the same place.
observations.soWhat: The most, the least and the same are read from the numbers, and how many more is the smaller taken from the larger.
observations.observe: Two numbers shared one place on the rail, and the most and the least stood at its two ends.

source_tool.description: A desk fills the stage. Along its top edge a drawn class of children waits, and tapping a child brings their answer down onto the desk as a slip, so the data is seen being collected one answer at a time. A ruled table stands in the middle of the desk with a heading cell for each answer and an empty number cell under each. The child drags each slip into the column for its name, where the number under that heading goes up by one. A total cell at the end of the table adds the numbers under the headings and is checked against the heap of slips it came from. A pictograph board can slide over the table: a title strip along its top, a key card beside it, and rows of symbols. Tapping a row counts its symbols one at a time into the running count, then takes the key that many times and writes the row's number, with its unit, at the end of the row. A compare rail stands the rows' numbers side by side from the largest to the smallest, so the most and the least can be read off its ends and two equal numbers stand level, and a total bar adds every row once the question asks for it.
source_tool.art_direction: A school desk under a drawn class / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a desk with a drawn class and a heap of answer slips, a ruled table, a tally board with a belt of answer cards, pictograph boards with a title strip and a key card, symbols that fold down their middle, a small route map, a tray of picture stamps, and a key dial.
Every pictograph carries a title strip at its top and a key card beside it from the first frame. A title or key still to be filled is an outlined blank, never a space left out.

Every symbol in one pictograph is one plain picture drawn at one size, evenly spaced from the same edge in every row or column, so a row's length is its count of symbols. A face, a kite, a cup, a tree or a bus; no letter, sign or mark ever stands in for a picture.

When the rows of a pictograph name colours, each row's symbols, whole or half, are drawn in that row's colour, and the key's symbol in plain grey. Otherwise every symbol in one pictograph, the key's included, is drawn in one colour.

A half symbol is the left half of the whole symbol, cut down its middle, as the chapter's own keys show it. It always comes last in its row. Halves are the only part of a symbol ever drawn, and only on a key that halves into whole things.
A tally mark is one short upright line. Every fifth mark is drawn across the four before it, corner to corner, and the next mark starts a new bundle after a small gap.
A pictograph drawn up the page stacks its symbols from the bottom. Its side is left unnumbered, or numbered only in the data's own units, the key times the symbols counted, and never in symbols.

The count of symbols and the number they stand for are never written in the same place: symbols are counted at the top left of the canvas, and a row's number is written at the end of its row with its unit.
The sum of every row is written under the board, labelled as the total for all the rows, and never beside a single row.
A row, a symbol or a mark is told apart by its name or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a tally mark, a symbol, a number, a band or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Every upright tally mark is deep blue, and the fifth mark, drawn across the four before it, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that counts in fives cannot afford a bundle whose closing mark has to be hunted for. Every pictograph symbol, whole or half, in the key and in every row, is green, except where the rows are told apart by colour: there every symbol in a row is that row's own colour, red, green, blue, yellow or purple, and the key's symbol is plain grey, a grey used for nothing else, because it stands for a symbol of any colour. What a row, a column or a tally stands for once it is read, the number written beyond a row's end, the numbers in a table, the numbers a side ruler writes in the data's own units, what half a symbol stands for, and what a key leaves over, is amber. A total of every row, and a thing that a total counts more than once, such as a stop two routes share, are reddish purple. The row a question asks about, and the stretch by which one row or tally reaches beyond another, are marked by a pale sky blue band behind the symbols or marks. Every table rule, row line, belt, bracket, outlined blank and card border is near-black chrome, and titles, row names, headings and the wording of every key are near-black type. All of that holds in greyscale, because a fifth mark lies across and not upright, a half symbol is the left half of the whole, a row's number sits beyond its end, a total sits in its own bar or cell, and a band lies behind a row rather than on it.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the name at the top of the column, and count that row again.
voice.onNext: Another question. Read the names before you read the numbers.
voice.opening: A class along the top, and an empty table on the desk. Ask each child.
voice.onFinish: Answers collected, set out under their names, read with the key, and compared.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any class and any question, with the table and the board open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Setting data out in a table
Reading a pictograph with its key
Most, least, equal and in all

placement.where: After the class has been asked how they came to school and the answers marked on the board, and before the recap's pictograph is read. The tool is what drops each answer into its column as it comes and adds the columns against the heap they came from, so a table is seen being made from collected facts rather than handed over.

answer_key.rule: Data is a collection of facts that gives useful information. Collected data is set out in a table with each number under its own name, and when each thing counted sits under one name only, the numbers under the names add up to the whole group. A pictograph row is read by counting its symbols and taking the key that many times. The most and the least are found by comparing the numbers, two rows with the same number are equal, and the total is every row added once.
answer_key.wrong: The slips are dropped into their columns again one at a time with the count said aloud, and a pictograph row is counted again symbol by symbol before the key is taken, so the child sees where the count and the number parted. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Data is a collection of facts that gives useful information.
The librarian collected four counts, each with the name of its class beside it, so each number says what it counts.
Read them: 31 is the largest, so Class 4B has the most. Each child is in one class, so 23 + 31 + 18 + 27 = 99 children have a card.
items.answer: Yes, it is data. It tells that Class 4B has the most card holders, 31, and that 99 children have a card in all
items.question: A librarian writes down how many children in each of four classes have a library card: Class 4A 23, Class 4B 31, Class 4C 18 and Class 4D 27. Is this data, and what can it tell the librarian?
items.checkpoint: Facts collected to give useful information are data.
items.misconception: Calling any list of numbers data even when nothing says what was counted, when a number gives information only with its name beside it.

steps: Write each season as a heading and its number of children under it.
Every number now sits under its own name, so none is mixed up with another.
Each child chose one season, so the numbers add up to the whole class: 6 + 9 + 8 + 5 = 28.
items.answer: A table with Summer 6, Rainy season 9, Winter 8 and Spring 5, and 28 children in all
items.question: Children in a class chose their favourite season. Summer was chosen by 6 children, the rainy season by 9, winter by 8 and spring by 5. Each child chose one season. Set this out in a table and find how many children there are.
items.checkpoint: In a table each number sits under its own name, and together they add up to the whole group.
items.misconception: Counting the four seasons and saying there are 4 children, instead of adding the numbers under them.

steps: Count the pictures in the row: there are 5.
Read the key: one picture stands for 6 mangoes.
items.question: A pictograph titled Mangoes Picked has the key one mango picture for 6 mangoes. The row for the tallest tree holds 5 mango pictures. How many mangoes were picked from that tree?
items.checkpoint: Count the pictures in a row, then multiply by what one picture stands for.
items.misconception: Writing 5, the number of pictures, as the number of mangoes, without using the key.

steps: Turn each row into a number with the key: 5 x 4 = 20, 8 x 4 = 32, 3 x 4 = 12 and 5 x 4 = 20.
Compare them: 32 is the most, 12 is the fewest, and 20 appears twice, for 4A and 4D.
Add every row for the total: 20 + 32 + 12 + 20 = 84 stickers.
items.answer: 4B the most, 32 stickers; 4C the fewest, 12; 4A and 4D the same, 20 each; 84 stickers in all
items.question: A pictograph of stickers collected by four classes has the key one star for 4 stickers. Class 4A has 5 stars, 4B has 8, 4C has 3 and 4D has 5. Which class collected the most, which the fewest, which two collected the same, and how many stickers were collected in all?
items.checkpoint: Compare the numbers for the most, the least and the same, and add them all for the total.
items.misconception: Adding the stars, 21, and giving that as the number of stickers, without using the key.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A class writes down each child's favourite colour. Is the list of answers data?
items.final_answer: Yes. It is a collection of facts that gives useful information: which colours the class likes

items.question: Which of these is data: the number of rainy days in each month of last year, or a drawing of a rain cloud?
items.final_answer: The number of rainy days in each month, because those are facts collected to give useful information

items.question: A table of the fruit children chose shows mango 7, guava 5, banana 9 and apple 4. Each child chose one fruit. How many children chose a fruit?
A class of 30 set out its favourite games in a table: kabaddi 8, cricket 11, football 6, and the cell for kho-kho left empty. Each child chose one game. What number goes in the kho-kho cell?
In a pictograph of pencils sold, one pencil picture stands for 10 pencils. A row holds 7 pencil pictures. How many pencils is that?
A pictograph of glasses of juice sold has the key one glass picture for 8 glasses. The rows for three days hold 2, 5 and 4 glass pictures. How many glasses were sold on each day?
A canteen sold 14 plates of idli on Monday, 9 on Tuesday, 14 on Wednesday and 11 on Thursday. On which day were the fewest sold, which two days sold the same, and how many plates were sold in all?
items.final_answer: Tuesday the fewest; Monday and Wednesday the same, 14 each; 48 plates in all

items.question: In a pictograph of trees planted by four houses, one tree picture stands for 5 trees. Ganga has 6 pictures, Yamuna 4, Kaveri 9 and Narmada 4. Which house planted the most trees, how many is that, and how many trees were planted in all?
items.final_answer: Kaveri, 45 trees; 115 trees in all, because 30 + 20 + 45 + 20 = 115

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: brings one child's answer down onto the desk as a slip when that child is tapped
holds the answers collected so far
sets a heading cell for each answer with a number cell under it
takes a slip into the column for its name and adds one under that heading
adds the numbers under the headings and checks them against the heap
slides over the table with a title strip, a key card and rows of symbols
counts a row's symbols and takes the key that many times
stands the rows' numbers side by side from the largest to the smallest
adds every row once, when the question asks for the total

teaching_notes: Ask the class how they came to school before the tool is opened, and mark each answer on the board as it comes. Then set the answers out in a table, add it up, and check the total against the number of children asked. The section of the chapter headed Data Collection defines data and then only sets out data already collected, twenty-six children in four houses, and no task in the chapter asks a child to collect anything, so let the class collect first. The table in that section heads its row team where the text says house and lists the houses in another order; every value agrees, so read it from the table. The recap reads a pictograph of the sixes hit by five cricketers, one bat for three sixes, and asks for the most, the least, the two that are equal and the total. The questions ask for sixes, not bats, so every row is turned into sixes with the key before an answer is given, and the total adds every row, which is right there because the question asks for all five together. Name nobody; call each row by what it counts.
generation_prompt: Build a data table tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A drawn class of up to thirty simple children stands along the top edge of the working area; tapping a child drops their answer onto the desk below as a labelled slip. A ruled table in the middle of the working area has a heading cell for each possible answer and an empty number cell under each; dragging a slip into a column adds one to the number under that heading, and a total cell at the end adds the numbers under the headings and is compared with the count of slips. A pictograph board can slide over the table, with a title strip across its top, a key card beside it showing one symbol and what it stands for, and rows of one symbol at one size, evenly spaced from the same left edge. Tapping a row counts its symbols one at a time into the running count at the top left of the canvas, then writes the row's number, with its unit, at the end of the row. A compare rail stands the rows' numbers side by side from the largest to the smallest, with equal numbers level. A total bar under the board adds every row once when tapped. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Tap each child to hear their answer. Drag each answer to its column. Add the columns. Count the pictures in a row. Use the key to find the number. Find the most, the least and the total.
